title: Babies, eggs and growing up
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Biology Unit 1.3 'Animal babies' (all animals have young; young grow into adults; some young look like their parents and some don't). No textbook needed.
summary: Your child finds out that every animal, and every person, began as something small: an egg, a baby or a seed. They learn the names of animal young, discover babies that look nothing like their parents (tadpoles and caterpillars), test how strong an eggshell is, and meet the many ways animals look after their young: mothers, fathers, aunties, whole villages, and baby turtles who never meet their mother at all. They grow a baby plant and measure it, and make a book of how they themselves have grown.
subconcepts: names for young: calf, kid, chick, cub, puppy, tadpole, caterpillar
some young look like their parents, some don't
metamorphosis: a big change (caterpillar to butterfly, tadpole to frog)
an egg carries food (the yolk) for the baby inside
many ways of caring: mothers, fathers, aunties, whole groups, or no care at all
what young need: food, water, warmth, safety (mammal babies drink milk)
human stages: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult, older person
how I have changed: height, teeth, what I can do
plants have young too: seeds and seedlings, which grow
builds_on: This is the first time. It sits beside 'What is alive?' (making young is a sign of life). In Class 2 your child comes back to measure growth, follow whole life cycles and ask why humans have such a long childhood; genes and inheriting features explain why young look like their parents.
goals: By the end your child can name the young of at least eight animals.
By the end your child can say that all animals have young and that the young grow into adults.
By the end your child can give two animals whose babies look like them and two whose babies don't, and describe how a caterpillar becomes a butterfly.
By the end your child can sort animals into those that lay eggs and those that are born alive.
By the end your child can describe three different ways animals look after (or don't look after) their young.
By the end your child can describe how they have grown and changed since they were a baby.
words: the babies of an animal or plant
a fully grown animal or person
a shell or jelly case with a baby animal growing inside
the yellow food inside an egg that the baby grows on
when a baby animal breaks out of their egg
the circle of egg or baby, young, adult, and new young
a big change in body shape as a young animal grows, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly
the hard case a caterpillar makes before they become a butterfly
an animal with hair or fur whose babies drink their mother's milk

days.title: Every animal was a baby
days.goal: Find out that all animals have young, and plant a baby plant.

steps.title: Who is this?
steps.do: Show your child a photo of themselves as a baby, or of a younger cousin. Ask: 'Who is this? What could this baby do? What can you do now?' (Walk, talk, eat idli by myself, ride a cycle.) Say: 'You were once a tiny baby. So was every animal: every dog, every crow, every elephant. This week we find out how animals grow up.'

steps.title: Baby names
steps.do: Say an adult animal and your child says the baby's name. Then swap. Cow (calf), dog (puppy), cat (kitten), hen (chick), goat (kid), horse (foal), lion and tiger (cub), elephant (calf), duck (duckling), frog (tadpole), butterfly (caterpillar), human (baby). If your child is stuck, give a clue: 'She says moo, and her baby is a…' Then do section A of Worksheet ws1 together.

steps.title: Plants have babies too
steps.do: Start Experiment e1. Ask: 'Do plants have babies?' Show a methi seed and say: 'A seed is a baby plant, resting. Let's plant some and watch them grow up.' Your child plants the seeds, waters them and puts the cup in a bright place. They make a name card for the cup.

need: a baby photo of your child

days.title: Do babies look like their parents?
days.goal: See that some young look like their parents and some don't.

steps.title: Seed check
steps.do: Look at the methi cup. Anything yet? Water it a little. Ask: 'When the seeds grow, will they look like the plant they came from?'

steps.title: Story: Run to the Bright Edge
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). A baby olive ridley turtle tells the story, on a beach in Odisha. Ask the questions after. Listen for: 'The mother put everything the baby needed into the egg' and 'The village kept the lights off.'

steps.title: Look-alike or not?
steps.do: Show pictures, in a book or on a phone, of these pairs: cat and kitten, cow and calf, duck and duckling, then frog and tadpole, butterfly and caterpillar. For each, ask: 'Does the baby look like their mother? What is the same? What is different?' Say: 'A kitten looks like a small cat. But a tadpole has a tail, no legs, and lives only in water. A caterpillar has no wings. These babies change a lot as they grow. A big change in body shape like this is called metamorphosis.' Your child says the word slowly and acts it: curl up small, then open out like wings.

need: pictures of animals and their babies (a book or phone)

days.title: Big changes: caterpillar to butterfly
days.goal: Follow the life cycle of a butterfly and a frog.

steps.title: Seed check
steps.do: Look at the methi cup. Have tiny shoots come up? Count them. Your child draws one.

steps.title: Life-cycle wheel
steps.do: Do Activity a1: make a butterfly life-cycle wheel on a paper plate with four stages: egg on a leaf, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. Tell the story as you draw: 'A butterfly lays a tiny egg on a leaf. A caterpillar hatches and eats and eats. As the caterpillar grows, they split their skin and grow a new, bigger one. Then the caterpillar hangs still inside a hard case called a chrysalis. Inside, their body changes completely. Out comes a butterfly, who lays eggs, and the cycle starts again.' Then tell the frog's life cycle: frogspawn (eggs in jelly), tadpole, tadpole with legs, froglet, frog. If you have a lemon or curry-leaf plant, look under the leaves for small caterpillars of the lime butterfly. Look, but don't pick them.

steps.title: Voice v1: the girl who watched caterpillars
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1, Maria Sibylla Merian. As a girl she raised caterpillars and painted every stage, at a time when many grown-ups thought insects grew out of mud. Ask: 'How did Merian find out that insects come from eggs?'

need: a split pin or a pencil to poke a hole

days.title: Eggs
days.goal: Find out what is inside an egg and which animals lay eggs.

steps.title: Seed check
steps.do: Look at the methi seedlings. Your child cuts a paper strip the same height as the tallest one and sticks it on a chart with today's date. Ask: 'Will the seedling be taller tomorrow?'

steps.title: The strong egg
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. First crack an egg into a bowl and look at the white and the yellow yolk. Keep it for cooking. Say: 'If a chick were growing in this egg, the yolk would be the chick's food until they hatch.' Then do the squeeze test with a second egg in a plastic bag over a bowl. Ask: 'Why does an egg need to be strong?' (So the mother can sit on it, and the baby is safe inside.) 'Then how does a chick get out?' (The chick has a tiny hard tip on their beak, called an egg tooth, to break the shell from inside.)

steps.title: Eggs or born alive?
steps.do: Say: 'Some babies hatch from eggs. Some are born alive, and drink their mother's milk: they are mammals.' Your child sorts: hen, crocodile, frog, butterfly, snake, sparrow, turtle (eggs); cow, dog, human, elephant, goat, cat (born alive). Ask: 'Which group drinks milk?' (The born-alive ones here: mammals.) Then do sections B and C of Worksheet ws1.

days.title: Who looks after the babies?
days.goal: Meet the many ways animals care for their young.

steps.title: Measure the seedling
steps.do: Cut a new paper strip for the tallest methi seedling and stick it next to yesterday's. Ask: 'Is the seedling taller? How do you know?'

steps.title: Many ways of caring
steps.do: Tell your child about these real animals. After each, ask: 'Who looks after the baby?' A cow licks her new calf and feeds the calf milk (the mother). A hen sits on her eggs to keep them warm, then shows the chicks what to peck (the mother). A mother crocodile guards her nest, then carries her hatchlings gently to the water in her mouth (the mother). The pheasant-tailed jacana is a bird of Indian lakes. The father sits on the eggs and guards the chicks, while the mother goes off to lay more eggs (the father). A seahorse father carries the eggs in a pouch until they hatch (the father). In an elephant herd the grandmother leads, and aunts and big sisters help look after the calves (the whole group). A turtle mother lays her eggs in the sand and goes back to the sea (nobody, but the egg holds what the baby needs). Ask: 'Which way is best?' Each way works for that animal. Then ask: 'What does every baby need, whoever looks after them?' Good answers: food (milk for mammal babies), water, warmth, a safe place, and for many, someone to learn from.

steps.title: Grow Up! board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1: race from egg to grown up, getting help and avoiding dangers. Read each square aloud when someone lands on it.

need: the printed board, a die and counters

days.title: How I have grown
days.goal: See the stages of a human life and how your child has changed.

steps.title: Measure the seedling
steps.do: Add today's paper strip for the methi. Line up all the strips: they make a little staircase. Ask: 'What does the staircase show?' (The plant grew taller each day.)

steps.title: Project: My Growing-Up Book
steps.do: Start the project. Lay out family photos, or draw them: a baby, a toddler, a child, a teenager, a grown-up, an older person. Your child puts them in order and names each stage. Ask: 'Which one are you?' On the first page of the book: a baby photo or drawing, their birth weight if you know it ('you weighed about as much as three packets of sugar'), and their first word. Say: 'Families are made in many ways. Babies are born into them, adopted, fostered or raised by grandparents. All are real families.' Ask: 'What could you do then? What can you do now?' Feel for a wobbly tooth or a gap: 'Milk teeth fall out and bigger teeth grow. That is growing too.'

steps.title: Voice v2: Jane and the chimp families
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2, Jane Goodall, who sat quietly in a forest for years watching chimpanzee mothers and babies. Ask: 'Jane gave the chimps names. Does naming an animal help you see them better?'

steps.title: Life-stage parade and lullaby
steps.do: Put on slow music. Call out each stage and your child acts it: a baby curled up and wriggling, a toddler wobbling, a child skipping, a teenager striding, a grown-up carrying a heavy bag, an older person walking slowly with a stick. Then your child rocks a soft toy and sings a lullaby your family knows. Ask: 'Why do we sing slow, soft songs to babies?' (Slow, soft songs help babies feel calm and fall asleep.)

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 (stretch). Read each item aloud. Your child points or answers aloud, and you write.

need: paper folded into a little book

days.title: Show and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the book, think about hard questions and teach what you know.

steps.title: The seedling staircase
steps.do: Look at the methi staircase chart. Ask: 'How did our seeds change?' (Seed, then a shoot, then leaves, then taller.) 'Are the plants grown up yet?' (No, they are young plants. One day they will flower and make seeds.) 'So does a plant have a life cycle too?' (Yes.)

steps.title: Finish the Growing-Up Book
steps.do: Finish the project: a page for 'Now' (height, a handprint, a favourite thing to do) and a page for 'When I am grown up'. Mark your child's height on a door frame with a pencil line and the date, so you can measure again in a year.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 (challenge) together. Read each question aloud. For the 'why' questions, write your child's own words. Any answer with a reason is a good answer.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child shows the family the Growing-Up Book and the life-cycle wheel, and teaches: 'All animals have young. Some look like their parents and some change a lot. Some hatch from eggs and some are born alive. Animals look after their young in different ways.' Then ask the check questions.

need: a pencil for the door frame

sections.p: Which is the right order for a butterfly?

the mother feeds her calf milk

sections.p: Hen's eggs from the shop don't hatch into chicks. Why?

their shells are too hard to break
they are kept in the light

Your child says, you write: A turtle mother lays about 100 eggs and leaves. A human mother usually has one baby and looks after the baby for years. Why do you think they are so different?
Your child says, you write: Do you think animal mothers love their babies? How could we find out?
Your child says, you write: If you were a caterpillar, what would you think was happening when you made your chrysalis?

experiments.title: Watch a baby plant grow up
experiments.question: How does a seed grow, and how fast?
need: a cup or small pot of soil
steps: Sprinkle about 20 methi seeds on the soil and cover them with a thin layer of soil.
Water gently and keep the cup in a bright place.
Water a little every day.
From Day 4, cut a paper strip as tall as the tallest seedling each day. Stick the strips side by side on the chart, with the date.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'How many days until we see a shoot? Will the seedlings grow the same amount every day?'
experiments.observe: Shoots in 2 to 3 days, then two small leaves, then more. The strips make a staircase.
experiments.why: A seed is a plant's young: a baby plant with a store of food. With water and warmth the seed wakes and grows: first a root down, then a shoot up, then leaves that make food from sunlight. Growing is more than getting bigger. The seedling also changes shape, just as a baby becomes a child.
experiments.time: 12 min + a few minutes a day for a week

experiments.title: The strong egg
experiments.question: How strong is an eggshell, and why?
steps: Crack one egg into a bowl and look at the white and the yolk. Keep it for cooking.
Check the second egg has no cracks. Put it inside the plastic bag.
Your child holds the egg in their palm, over the bowl, and wraps their whole hand around the egg.
Squeeze hard and evenly with the whole hand. Take off any rings, and don't poke with fingertips.
Then a grown-up shows how a gentle tap on the edge of the bowl cracks it easily.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Can you break the egg by squeezing it in your hand?'
experiments.observe: Squeezed evenly, the egg usually doesn't break; tapped on one spot, it cracks.
experiments.why: The egg's curved shape spreads a push all over the shell, so the shell is very strong when pressed evenly, strong enough for a hen to sit on. But a sharp push on one small spot, like a tap or a chick's egg tooth from inside, cracks the shell. The shell protects the baby, the yolk feeds the baby, and tiny holes in the shell let air in so the baby can breathe.
experiments.safety: Do it over a bowl inside a bag. Wash hands with soap after touching raw egg.

activities.title: Butterfly life-cycle wheel
need: a split pin or a pencil
steps: Draw two lines across the plate to make four parts.
In each part draw one stage: egg on a leaf, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly.
Draw arrows going round from one to the next.
Pin the paper arrow in the middle so the arrow spins.
Spin the arrow and tell the story of each stage. On the back, draw the frog's life cycle: frogspawn, tadpole, froglet, frog.
activities.outcome: A spinning life-cycle wheel your child can use to tell the story of metamorphosis.

project.title: My Growing-Up Book
steps: Fold 3 sheets of paper in half to make a small book.
Page 1: Me as a baby (photo or drawing, birth weight, first word).
Page 2: Me as a toddler (what I could do).
Page 3: Me now (height, a handprint, a favourite thing to do).
Page 4: The stages of a human life, in order.
Page 5: When I am grown up.
Mark today's height on a door frame with the date.
project.outcome: A little book showing how your child has grown and changed, and a height mark to measure against next year.

game.title: Grow Up!
rules: Everyone starts on EGG. Take turns to roll the die and move.
Read the square aloud and do what it says.
The first to reach GROWN UP! wins, and says which baby animal they would like to be.
squares: EGG
You hatch! Move on 1
Your mother keeps you warm. Move on 2
A crow looks at you. Go back 1
Drink milk. Move on 1
Say the name of a baby cow, then move on 1
Hide in the grass from a hawk. Stay where you are.
You shed your skin to grow. Move on 2
Rain! Shelter under a leaf. Stay where you are.
Your father guards you. Move on 2
Aunty elephant helps you cross the river. Move on 3
You wandered off. Go back 2
Eat lots of leaves. Move on 1
Name an animal that lays eggs. Move on 1
Make a chrysalis. Miss a turn while you change.
You grow legs! Move on 2
The beach lights are off, so you find the sea. Move on 2
Name a baby that looks different from their parent. Move on 1
Sleep well: children grow while they sleep. Move on 1
Learn to find food. Move on 2
GROWN UP!

big: Why does a human baby need looking after for years, when a baby turtle needs no one?
Is a caterpillar the same animal as the butterfly they become?
Do animal mothers and fathers love their babies?
You were once one tiny cell, smaller than a full stop. How did you get so big?
Which is better: lots of babies and no care, or one baby and lots of care?

challenge.q: In a famous picture book, a hungry caterpillar builds a cocoon and comes out a butterfly. Is that right?
challenge.hint: Not quite. A butterfly caterpillar makes a hard case called a chrysalis. A moth caterpillar spins a soft silk case called a cocoon. Even good books can get things wrong. How could you check what a book says?

challenge.q: People say: 'If you touch a baby bird, its mother will smell you and leave it.' Is that true?
challenge.hint: No. Most birds have a weak sense of smell, and scientists have found that parents don't leave chicks just because a person touched them. But we still shouldn't touch nests. It frightens the parents and can lead cats or crows to the nest. A rule can be good even when the reason people give for it is wrong.

challenge.q: 'Mothers look after babies.' Is it always the mother?
challenge.hint: No. Jacana and seahorse fathers do the caring, and elephant aunts help. In many human families, fathers, grandparents and neighbours share the work. Who looks after babies in your family and your street?

perspectives.view: A koel mother lays her eggs in a crow's nest, and the crows raise the koel chick as their own. People sometimes call the koel lazy or a cheat. Ask: is that fair? What does the crow lose? What might the koel say?

In an elephant herd the oldest female leads. She remembers where to find water in a dry year, and the whole family helps raise each calf. Ask: why might the oldest elephant be the best leader in a dry year?

Olive ridley turtles also nest on the beaches of Chennai, from January to March. Every year volunteers walk the beaches at night, move the eggs to a safe fenced hatchery, and let the hatchlings go into the sea. Ask: whose babies are these turtles? Who should look after them?

voices.who: Maria Sibylla Merian (1647–1717), Germany and the Netherlands
voices.idea: From the age of 13 Merian raised silkworms and other caterpillars and painted every stage: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis or cocoon, adult, and the plant each one ate. Many people then believed insects simply appeared out of mud or rotting things. At 52 she sailed to Suriname in South America with her daughter Dorothea to study insects there, and published a great book of paintings, 'Metamorphosis of the Insects of Suriname' (1705).
voices.then: She was a woman with no university training, and for a long time scientists treated her more as an artist than a scientist. Some later writers doubted her observations.
voices.now: Her observations of insect life cycles are accepted, and she is now honoured as one of the first people to study how animals change as they grow, and how they live with the plants they eat.
voices.ask: People thought insects came from mud. How did Merian find out that insects come from eggs? What would you need to watch to be sure?

voices.who: Jane Goodall (1934–2025), England, working in Tanzania
voices.idea: In 1960, without a university degree, Goodall began watching chimpanzees at Gombe in Tanzania. She sat quietly for years until the chimps trusted her. She saw that chimp mothers carry, feed, play with and teach their babies for years, that young chimps learn by watching, and that each chimp has their own character.
voices.then: Some scientists criticised her for giving the chimps names instead of numbers and for saying they had feelings and personalities.
voices.now: Her findings are accepted; long childhoods and learning from mothers are now known in chimps, elephants, whales and many birds. Scientists still discuss how to study animal feelings carefully.
voices.ask: Jane gave the chimps names, like Flo and David Greybeard. Some scientists said that was not scientific. What do you think? Does naming an animal help you see them better, or make you see what you want to see?

story.title: Run to the Bright Edge
text: Before I had eyes, I had an egg. The egg was round and white, with a soft, leathery shell, about as big as a lime. It was buried deep in the sand of a beach called Rushikulya, in Odisha, beside the sea. I didn't know any of those names then. I knew only warm, and dark, and the slow, steady feeling of growing.

Inside my egg there was a golden ball of food, the yolk, and I lived on it. Every day the sun warmed the sand above me and every night it cooled, and every day I was a little bigger and the golden ball was a little smaller. I grew a shell on my back. I grew four flippers. I grew a beak the size of a grain of rice, with a tiny hard point on the tip. I didn't know what the point was for. I would soon.
All around me in the dark were my brothers and sisters, more than a hundred of us, each in our own egg, each growing. We could not see each other. But sometimes I felt them move.
I did not count the days. Turtles in eggs don't count. But after about fifty of them the golden ball was gone, and I was folded so tight I could hardly turn, and something inside me said: now.

I pushed with the hard point of my beak, and the egg tore. Sand pressed in. Around me my brothers and sisters were tearing their eggs too. We wriggled and scratched. The ones on top scraped the sand down from the ceiling, the ones below pressed it flat on the floor, and slowly, all together, the whole nest of us rose up through the sand, the way water rises in a well. Not one of us could have done it alone.
Near the top the sand was hot from the day, and we stopped. Something inside me said: not yet. So we waited, packed together, until the sand went cool. Then, at night, we burst out.
Stars. Wind. A great roaring I had never heard before. And a girl.

She was crouched beside our nest with a torch pointed at the ground. Her name was Lipi. All through the hatching season she and the other volunteers from her village sat up at night on the beach, chasing away dogs and crows from the nests. Beside her was a small boy, her brother Jitu, who had begged to come.
"They're out!" whispered Lipi. "Look, Jitu, look!"
Jitu looked at us. We were no bigger than matchboxes, scrambling over each other on the sand. Then he looked up and down the empty beach.
"Where's their mother?" he said. "Shouldn't their mother be here?"

"She came in the spring, at night, with thousands of other mothers," said Lipi. "She dug a hole with her back flippers, laid her eggs, covered them with sand, and went back into the sea. That was nearly two months ago."
Jitu's face crumpled. "So nobody looks after them? Nobody shows them the way?"

I didn't know the way. I had never seen anything at all. But when my head came out of the sand, I looked. In one direction the world was dark: the land, the casuarina trees, the sleeping village. In the other direction it was a little brighter, where the moonlight and starlight lay on the moving water. And something inside me said: run to the bright edge.

I ran. My flippers had never run before, but they knew how. Sand, then wet sand, then a crab that scuttled sideways, then more sand. A dog came trotting down the beach and Lipi jumped up and waved her arms until it ran off.
"How do the babies know where to go?" asked Jitu.
"Their mother told them," said Lipi.
"But she isn't here!"

"She told them before," said Lipi. "She put everything they need into the egg. The yolk to grow on. The hard point on the beak to break out. The flippers. And the knowing: run to the brightest part of the sky, because that's the sea." She switched her torch off. "That's why we turn the lights off on the beach road at hatching time. If there's a bright light on the land, the babies run the wrong way."
Jitu thought about that. Then he reached over and switched off the little torch hanging round his own neck.
The first wave hit me like a wall. It rolled me over and pulled me back, and then the water lifted me, and I was swimming. I had never swum, but I knew how.

I am far out at sea now. I eat small crabs and jellyfish, and I am growing, the way I grew in the egg, a little every day. In many years, when I am grown, something inside me will say: now. And I will swim back across the sea to the beach where I was an egg. I don't know how I will find it. Nobody quite knows.
I will dig a hole with my back flippers, and lay my eggs, each with its golden ball of food, and cover them, and go back into the sea before they wake.
And on that beach, I hope, there will be a girl with her torch switched off, waiting.
story.epiphany: Animals look after their young in many different ways. The turtle mother never meets her babies, but she gives them everything in the egg: the yolk to grow on, the egg tooth to hatch, and the instinct to run to the bright sea. The turn is Lipi's answer, 'She told them before.' Underneath: the hatchlings can only dig out together, and a whole village chooses to care for babies that are not their own. The life cycle closes as the grown turtle comes back to lay eggs.
ask: What did the baby turtle eat inside the egg?
Why couldn't one baby turtle have dug out of the sand alone?
How did the turtle know which way to run?
Jitu was sad that the mother had gone. Was anyone looking after the babies?
Why did Jitu switch off his torch?

ideas.idea: Every animal starts small and grows.
ideas.more: An elephant, a crow, a crocodile and you each began as one tiny egg cell. Put an egg yolk, a baby photo and a methi seedling side by side: three beginnings.

ideas.idea: Growing up can mean changing completely.
ideas.more: A caterpillar and a butterfly are the same animal. A tadpole lives in water and breathes there, and the frog the tadpole becomes breathes air. Growing up means changing shape, not just getting bigger.

ideas.idea: There are many ways to care for young.
ideas.more: Mothers, fathers, aunts, grandmothers, whole herds and whole villages care for young. Some mothers, like the turtle, put everything the baby needs into the egg. Ask your child who cared for them, and who they could help care for.

unknowns: How do baby turtles find their way back, years later, to the beach where they hatched? Scientists think they may remember the Earth's magnetism there, but nobody is sure.

Does a butterfly remember anything from being a caterpillar? Some experiments with moths show that a little learning lasts through the change. Nobody knows what the change feels like to the caterpillar.
Do animal parents feel love for their young the way people do? We can watch what they do, but we can't yet see inside their feelings.

books.author: P.D. Eastman
books.why: A baby bird hatches alone and goes looking for his mother: a funny way into who cares for babies.

check.q: What is a baby cow called? A baby frog? A baby butterfly?
check.a: A calf, a tadpole, a caterpillar.

check.q: Name an animal whose baby looks like their parent, and one whose baby looks very different.
check.a: For example, a kitten looks like a cat, but a tadpole looks very different from a frog.

check.q: What are the stages of a butterfly's life?
Name two animals that hatch from eggs and two that are born alive.
check.a: For example, a hen and a crocodile hatch from eggs. A cow and a human are born alive.

check.q: What does a chick eat while the chick is inside the egg?
Tell me two different ways animals look after their young.
check.a: For example, a cow feeds her calf milk, a seahorse father carries the eggs, and a turtle mother puts everything the baby needs into the egg.

check.q: How have you changed since you were a baby?
check.a: I am taller and heavier, I have more teeth, and I can walk, talk and eat by myself.
